text: A technically accurate SOC report — parsed 1.2 billion events, fired 3,814 alerts, escalated 12 true positives — is correct, and it tells an executive almost nothing. Leadership isn't equipped to judge whether 3,814 is a good number, and they don't need to be. Their job is deciding whether the SOC is reducing business risk and needs more investment to keep doing so.

The same month, reported differently: the SOC identified and blocked 12 attempted breaches this month, and average detection time improved 18% compared to last quarter, meaning attackers had less time inside the environment before being caught. It's the same underlying data — those 12 true positives, that MTTD trend from Lesson 22 — reframed around what leadership actually decides on.

Three things consistently belong in a leadership report: a plain-language risk statement framed around what could have happened, not a log count; a trend rather than a snapshot, since quarter-over-quarter movement in MTTD, MTTR, or the workload numbers from Lesson 23 is what shows real change; and a specific ask tied to a number, like staffing that can't sustain current workload past next quarter.

A SOC's budget and headcount aren't renewed because leadership trusts security is important in the abstract. They're renewed because someone made a specific, numeric case — built directly from the detection, response, and workload trends covered in the last two lessons — translated into language a non-technical decision-maker can actually act on.

A SOC that reports this way consistently, month after month, builds the credibility that makes the next budget conversation easier, not harder. That closes the triage-to-leadership chain this chapter has been building — and it sets up Chapter 7, which turns to SOAR: automating the repeatable parts of that response so analysts can spend their time on the judgment calls that actually need it.
